alt: The Human Rights Act is pulled two ways. Those wanting less judicial or European influence point to section 3 rewriting statutes (Ghaidan), section 2 and the Ullah mirror principle, prisoner voting after Hirst, and expanding obligations. Those wanting stronger protection point to no entrenchment, non-binding section 4 declarations, no social rights and gaps in section 6 (YL v Birmingham).
caption: Every reform option answers one side’s criticisms and sharpens the other’s.

alt: A table of five options ordered from less external check to stronger protection: withdraw from the Convention, replace the HRA with a UK Bill of Rights while staying in the Convention, amend sections 2 and 3, keep the HRA unchanged, or strengthen protection by entrenchment, a written constitution or social rights, each with supporters’ case and objections.
caption: Replacing the HRA is not the same as leaving the Convention.

alt: A timeline: the Commission on a Bill of Rights (2011 to 2012) found majority support in principle but no agreed content; the 2015 manifesto pledged to scrap the HRA; the Independent Human Rights Act Review (2020 to 2021) found it working broadly well; the Bill of Rights Bill was introduced in June 2022 and dropped in June 2023; the Safety of Rwanda Act 2024 disapplied parts of the HRA before the policy was abandoned.
caption: Repeal has been proposed repeatedly, but the HRA remains in force.

alt: Four constraints around “changing the HRA”: devolution statutes make incompatible devolved acts outside competence, entrenching the HRA in the settlement; the Sewel Convention, though not legally enforceable; the Belfast (Good Friday) Agreement’s commitment to incorporate the Convention in Northern Ireland; and Article 46, binding the UK to final Strasbourg judgments.
caption: Devolution, Northern Ireland and Article 46 limit what Westminster can do alone.

alt: A timeline of Strasbourg reform: Protocol 14 in force in 2010 with single-judge decisions and the significant disadvantage criterion; the Interlaken conference in 2010; the Brighton conference in 2012, whose Declaration led to Protocol 15; and Protocol 15 in force in 2021, adding subsidiarity and the margin of appreciation to the preamble and cutting the time limit from six months to four.
caption: Strasbourg has reformed itself to give national authorities more room.

after: ## Annotated plan: "Discuss whether the Human Rights Act 1998 should be replaced by a UK Bill of Rights."
alt: An essay plan: an introduction setting out the HRA model; the case for replacement (Ghaidan, Ullah, Hirst, evaluated with Horncastle); the case against (Article 46 and the Independent Review’s findings); constraints from devolution and the Belfast Agreement; alternative reforms; and a conclusion, for example preferring targeted amendment.
caption: A sustained argument weighing options against the criticisms they are meant to fix.
